    Synthesis, Characterization, and Evaluation of
 Antimicrobial Double-Layer Mat Incorporating Nisin
   and Thyme Essential Oil to Enhance Food Safety

  Niloofar Shirdam1, Mohammad Mir-Derikvand1*, Ali Hossein Rezayan1, and
                            Mahsa Kalantar1
  1School of Life Science Engineering, College of Interdisciplinary Science and

                 Technology, University of Tehran, Tehran, Iran

            *Corresponding Author E-mail: mohammad.mir@ut.ac.ir



Abstract
Antimicrobial active packaging is a promising strategy to control foodborne
contamination, yet the instability and rapid inactivation of natural preservatives


                                                S S
in complex food matrices limit their practical use. Here, we fabricate and evaluate
an electrospun double-layer nanobiocomposite mat engineered to protect

                                             R E
bioactives and enable their slow release. The inner layer comprises chitosan/poly

                                            P
(vinyl alcohol) loaded with nisin and Shirazi thyme essential oil (CS/PVA/N/EO),


                                     IN
while the outer layer is cellulose acetate containing thyme essential oil (CA/EO).
Solutions were electrospun and characterized by SEM, FTIR, TGA, contact angle,

                          L E
and tensile testing; antibacterial performance was assessed by agar diffusion and

                       IC
a dynamic shake-flask assay. SEM revealed bead-free fibers in the inner layer with


                    RT
an average diameter of 144.8 ± 28.33 nm. FTIR and TGA confirmed successful
incorporation of actives and thermal stability within typical processing ranges.
                  A
Surface wettability was asymmetric by design: the inner layer was hydrophilic
(contact angle 46.53°–72.43°) to promote release, whereas the outer CA/EO
surface was hydrophobic (95.5°) to resist moisture. The double-layer exhibited
adequate mechanical integrity for handling and conversion with an elongation at
break of 21.66 ± 0.62%. Antimicrobial tests confirmed inhibitory activity against
both Listeria monocytogenes (L. monocytogenes) and Escherichia coli (E. coli),
with inhibition zones reaching 27.26 ± 1.60 mm for L. monocytogenes and 25.13
± 1.40 mm for E. coli. In the dynamic assay, a 5 × 5 cm, 0.36 mm pad reduced L.
monocytogenes by 2 logs and maintained counts below the detection limit for 48
h, whereas the control increased to 9.58 ± 0.31 log CFU/mL. These results
demonstrate an effective active mat with potential application as an antimicrobial
liner.

Keywords: Electrospinning, Chitosan, Poly (vinyl alcohol), Cellulose acetate,
Nisin, Shirazi thyme essential oil.

1. Introduction

Food-borne pathogens represent one of the major global challenges to public
health and food safety. According to the World Health Organization (WHO),
contaminated food accounts for approximately 600 million cases of foodborne
illness and 420,000 deaths each year worldwide. Notably, nearly 30% of these
deaths occur in children under five years of age [1]. Furthermore, according to
the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), approximately 1,600 cases
of listeriosis are reported annually in the United States, leading to nearly 260
deaths [2].
These microorganisms not only pose a serious threat to human health but also
impose significant economic burdens on the food industry, particularly through
product recalls. For example, in 2023 the U.S. Food and Drug Administration

                                                   S
(FDA) recalled more than 400 products due to potential Listeria contamination
                                                 S
                                                E
[3]. Listeria monocytogenes (L. monocytogenes) is a pathogenic bacterium that


                                             PR
can cause severe illness, particularly in pregnant women, newborns, and
immunocompromised individuals. Infection typically occurs through the

                                      IN
consumption of contaminated foods. This bacterium is able to grow over a wide

                             E
range of conditions, including temperatures from 1 to 45 °C, pH values between

                           L
4.6 and 9.6, and high salt concentrations, making it extremely difficult to

                         C
                        I
eliminate from foods and food processing environments [4]. Therefore,

                      T
researchers are actively seeking strategies to control this pathogen, with
                     R
                   A
electrospinning technology for antimicrobial active packaging emerging as a
promising approach. Recent reports by Zhang et al. (2024) and Wang et al. (2024)
indicate that publications on this subject have increased substantially since 2017,
reflecting the growing scientific and industrial interest in applying
electrospinning technology within the food sector [5, 6].
In addition to microbiological risks, plastic waste from conventional food
packaging poses a major environmental challenge. The packaging sector
represents nearly half of global plastic production, which increased from 322
million tonnes in 2015 to 359 million tonnes in 2018, yet only about 9% is recycled
while 79% accumulates in landfills or ecosystems. Approximately 14-15 million
tonnes of this plastic enter the oceans each year, threatening marine life and food
chains.      These impacts underscore the urgent need for sustainable,
biodegradable, and antimicrobial packaging solutions to minimize plastic
pollution and improve food safety [7, 8].
Recent investigations by Dai et al. (2022), Yu et al. (2023), Guan et al. (2024), and
Li et al. (2024) have explored the potential of electrospinning technology for

ACCEPTED
                           ARTICLEMANUSCRIPT
                                   IN PRESS
developing active antimicrobial food packaging materials. These studies reported
encouraging outcomes, including effective inhibition of bacterial growth and
extension of food shelf life. Nevertheless, additional research is required to
optimize the design and functionality of such systems before they can be widely
adopted in the food industry [9-12]. Antimicrobial-active food packaging
incorporates bioactive ingredients and polymers capable of inhibiting or killing
bacteria, including L. monocytogenes. Micro and nano-encapsulation of these
bioactive compounds can protect them from inactivation by factors such as
enzymes. Consequently, the use of biological preservatives reduces the reliance
on chemical preservatives [13, 14].
Electrospinning is a scalable and reproducible technique that employs an electric
field to generate continuous nanofibers from a polymer solution. This method
enables the fabrication of food packaging materials capable of providing a
sustained release of antimicrobial agents over time [15]. Unlike conventional film-
forming approaches (such as casting, dip-coating, or extrusion) and fiber-forming
methods (such as spray drying and melt spinning), which typically require high
processing temperatures, electrospinning allows the incorporation of thermo-
sensitive bioactive compounds into the polymer matrix without degradation [16].
Additional advantages of this technique include the ability to control porosity and

                                                 S S
nanofiber diameters, as well as the production of structures with a high specific
surface area [6, 17].

                                              R E
On the other hand, nisin is a polypeptide bacteriocin produced by Lactococcus
                                             P
lactis, and it has been employed as a natural preservative in the food industry

                                      IN
since the 1950s [18]. However, its antimicrobial activity can be reduced through


                           L E
interactions with food components such as proteolytic enzymes and fat
compounds [19]. To achieve the desired antimicrobial effect, large amounts of

                        IC
nisin are often required, which is not only costly but may also encourage the

                     RT
development of resistant bacterial subpopulations [20]. Several studies have

                   A
suggested that incorporating nisin into microcapsules, liposomes, or nanofibers,
and co-encapsulating it with other antimicrobial agents such as essential oils, can
enhance its bioactivity and protect it from inactivation [21]. Thyme essential oil is
rich in phenolic compounds like thymol and carvacrol, is widely recognized for its
natural antimicrobial and antioxidant properties, making it an effective natural
preservative for food products [22]. Studies have shown that thyme essential oil
exhibits strong antimicrobial activity against various foodborne pathogens,
including Listeria monocytogenes [23]. The combination of nisin and thymol
enhanced antibacterial activity against Listeria monocytogenes and Bacillus
subtilis, allowing effective control with lower nisin levels and reducing the risk of
resistant sub-populations [24]. Moreover, research demonstrates a synergistic
antimicrobial effect when combining nisin (a bacteriocin) with thyme essential oil
against L. monocytogenes, enhancing the preservation effect [25]. Furthermore,
the combined effect of carvacrol, thymol, and nisin against Staphylococcus aureus
and Salmonella Enteritidis showed significant inhibition of these pathogens. This
supports the antimicrobial potential of combining thymol with nisin [26].

                                  IN PRESS
Therefore, in this study, we incorporated both nisin and thyme essential oil into
electrospun nanofibers. Building on our previous works in nanomaterial synthesis
and their applications in biomedical fields [27-31], the present study aimed to
fabricate electrospun double-layer mats with broad-spectrum antimicrobial
activity against both L. monocytogenes and E. coli. The inner layer was designed
as a hydrophilic CS/PVA nanofiber matrix loaded with nisin and Shirazi thyme
essential oil, while the outer layer consisted of a hydrophobic cellulose
acetate/thyme essential oil film. This novel double-layer design with asymmetric
wettability was intended to promote directional and sustained release of bioactive
compounds. Furthermore, the co-encapsulation of nisin and thyme essential oil
was designed to exploit their synergy, extending antimicrobial activity from L.
monocytogenes to E. coli. The mats were characterized for morphology,
physicochemical, and mechanical properties, and their antibacterial efficacy was
evaluated.

   2.2.     Preparation of Electrospinning Solutions

      2.2.1.      Preparation of the First Layer Solution (CA/EO Sample)

To prepare the first-layer solution, cellulose acetate (16% w/v) was dissolved in a
solvent mixture of acetone and dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) at a 1:2 ratio.
Subsequently, thyme essential oil (3% w/v) was added to the solution and stirred
for 1 h at room temperature [32].

      2.2.2.      Preparation of the Second Layer Solution (CS/PVA/N/EO)

To prepare the second-layer solution, poly (vinyl alcohol) (11% w/v) was dissolved
in deionized water under magnetic stirring at 90 °C for 1 h. Separately, chitosan
(2% w/v) was dissolved in acetic acid and stirred for 30 min, after which nisin was
added at a concentration of 15 mg/mL and mixed for an additional 30 min. After

the chitosan/nisin solution at a 30:70 ratio and stirred for 1 h. Subsequently,
thyme essential oil (3% w/v) was added to the mixture and stirred for 30 min.

   2.3.          Synthesis of Electrospun Nanofiber (Electrospinning Process)

An electrospinning device (Nanomeghyas, Iran) was employed, with solutions
separately loaded into 3 mL syringes (16-gauge needles) and mounted on a
syringe pump. For fabrication of the double-layer sample, the CA/EO layer was

ACCEPTED
                          ARTICLEMANUSCRIPT
                                  IN PRESS
electrospun first, followed immediately by the second nanofibrous layer. The
optimized electrospinning parameters for the first layer were an applied voltage
of 15 kV, a flow rate of 1 mL/h, and a needle-to-collector distance of 15 cm. For
the second layer, the optimal conditions were a voltage of 28 kV, a flow rate of
0.5 mL/h, and a needle-to-collector distance of 15 cm.

  2.4.     Scanning Electron Microscopy (SEM)

The morphology of the films (1 × 1 cm) was examined using scanning electron
microscopy (FEI ESEM QUANTA 200) after coating the samples with a thin layer
of gold via PVD sputtering (COXEM, South Korea). Average fiber diameters were
measured using ImageJ software, and the diameter distribution was analyzed by
fitting a Gaussian curve with OriginLab software.

  2.5.     Fourier Transform Infrared Spectroscopy (FTIR and ATR-FTIR)

FT-IR spectra of chitosan powder, nisin, and thyme essential oil, as well as ATR-
FTIR spectra of PVA, cellulose acetate, and nanofiber samples, were recorded in
the wavenumber range of 500–4000 cm⁻¹ using a PerkinElmer FTIR


                                               S S
spectrometer. The analysis was performed to identify functional groups and
assess potential structural interactions among the polymers and active
substances.

  2.7.     Water Contact Angle

Water contact angle measurements of CS/PVA, CS/PVA/N, CS/PVA/N/EO, and
double-layer samples were performed using a CA-500A contact angle analyzer
(Sharif Solar, Iran) following the static sessile drop method at room temperature.
A 12 μL droplet of distilled water was carefully placed on the surface of each
sample, and images were captured with a high-resolution camera. The contact
angles were then analyzed using ImageJ software.

  2.8.  Mechanical Testing Method and Thickness Measurement of the
     Samples

The mechanical properties of the electrospun mats were evaluated by tensile
testing using a universal testing machine (Santam Co., Iran). Rectangular
specimens with dimensions of 5.5 × 2.5 cm were prepared and clamped in the

ACCEPTED

grips of the tester. The tests were conducted at a crosshead speed of 5 mm/min
under ambient conditions. Tensile strength (TS), Young’s modulus (YM), and
elongation at break (EB) were calculated from the stress–strain curves. The
thickness of the samples was measured using a digital micrometer (Mitutoyo Co.,
Japan) with an accuracy of 0.001 mm. For each specimen, measurements were
taken at three different points, and the average value was reported [34].


   2.9.      Antibacterial Activity Assay

The antimicrobial activity of the nanobiocomposite mats against Listeria
monocytogenes (ATCC 19111) and Escherichia coli O157:H7 was evaluated using
the agar diffusion and dynamic shake-flask methods.

      2.9.1.        Agar Diffusion (Qualitative Measurement)

Agar diffusion tests were employed to qualitatively assess the presence and
activity of antimicrobial compounds. In this study, the antimicrobial properties of
the mats against L. monocytogenes and E. coli were evaluated following the Kirby-

                                                        S

                                                      S
strains in Mueller-Hinton Broth under sterile conditions and incubating at 37 °C

with 5% blood (for L. monocytogenes). Square mats (1 × 1 cm) were carefully

            Morphology of the Electrospun Nanofibers
                      R
                    A
Figures 2 and 3 present the scanning electron microscopy (SEM) images of the
electrospun mats. Figure 2 shows SEM images of three nanofiber samples:
chitosan/poly (vinyl alcohol) (CS/PVA), CS/PVA with nisin (CS/PVA/N), and
CS/PVA with nisin and essential oil (CS/PVA/N/EO). All samples exhibited uniform
fiber distribution with no bead formation. The mean diameter of CS/PVA
nanofibers was 125.7 ± 18.97 nm, which is consistent with previous reports. For
instance, Hedayatyanfard. et al. (2019) reported a diameter of 104 ± 24.99 nm
for nanofibers containing 3% chitosan and 5% PVA (80:20 ratio) [37]. Mei et al.
(2019) observed a mean diameter of 118.49 ± 10 nm for nanofibers of 3% chitosan
and 8% PVA (50:50 ratio) [38]. Similarly, Sosiati et al. (2020) reported 198 nm for
nanofibers of 3% chitosan and 10% PVA (80:20 ratio) [39], while Agrawal and
Pramanik (2016) found 264 nm for nanofibers prepared from 2% chitosan and
10% PVA (30:70 ratio) [33].
Accordingly, the diameter of chitosan–PVA nanofibers has generally been
reported in the range of 100–270 nm, with variations attributed to factors such as

polymer concentration, viscosity, and molecular weight. Upon the addition of 3%
nisin (CS/PVA/N), the fiber diameter increased significantly to 142.60 ± 28.14 nm

   3.2.     FTIR Analysis

Figure 4A shows the FTIR spectrum of nisin. The broad band at 3268 cm⁻¹ arises


                                                  S S
from O–H/N–H stretching. The band near 2900 cm⁻¹ corresponds to symmetric
and asymmetric C–H stretching vibrations. The peak at 1677 cm⁻¹ is assigned to

                                               R E
Amide I (C=O stretching) of peptide bonds, while the band at ~1540–1560 cm⁻¹

                                              P
(weak in this spectrum) represents Amide II (N–H bending + C–N stretching). The


                                       IN
signal at 1033 cm⁻¹ is attributed to C–O/C–N stretching.
Figure 4B illustrates the infrared spectrum of Shirazi thyme essential oil. Thymol

                           L E
is the main component of this essential oil, but it also contains other phenolic

                        IC
compounds. The peak at wavenumber 3537 cm-1 represents the stretching


                     RT
vibration of the hydroxyl group (O–H). The strong peak at wavenumber 2962 cm-
1 is attributed to C–H vibrations in aromatic compounds, while peaks at

                   A
wavenumbers 2927 cm-1 and 2870 cm-1 represent symmetric and asymmetric
stretching vibrations of CH3 groups. The presence of peaks in the range of 1516
cm-1 to 1619 cm-1 indicating C=C stretching vibration, confirms the presence of
aromatic rings .The bending vibrations within and out of the plane of the aromatic
rings result in peaks in the range of 1459 cm-1 to 1257 cm-1. The FTIR results for
Shirazi thyme essential oil are consistent with those reported by Catauro et al
[40].
ATR-FTIR spectra of CS, PVA, CS/PVA, CS/PVA/N, and CS/PVA/N/EO are shown
in Figures 4C–G. All samples display a broad O–H band, which becomes broader
in the nanofibrous mats due to hydrogen bonding and overlap with N–H vibrations
of chitosan, as described by Choo et al. [41]. The symmetric and asymmetric
stretching vibrations of C–H (CH2) can be observed in the chitosan, poly (vinyl
alcohol), and nanofibrous samples at wavenumbers of around 2900 cm-1. A
carbonyl band at ~1731–1715 cm⁻¹ is observed in PVA-containing samples,
originating from residual acetate groups of PVA; its slight shift and intensity

   3.4.     Contact Angle Test (Surface Wettability)

The degree of surface hydrophilicity or hydrophobicity is commonly evaluated by
the contact angle test. A contact angle greater than 90° indicates a hydrophobic
surface, whereas a lower value reflects a hydrophilic surface. As shown in Figure
7, the contact angle of CS/PVA nanofibers, which are inherently hydrophilic
polymers, was measured at 46.53°. Upon incorporation of nisin protein, the
contact angle increased significantly to 64.5° (p < 0.05). Further addition of 3%
thyme essential oil raised the contact angle to 72.43°, attributable to the
hydrophobic and oily characteristics of thyme essential oil. A similar trend was

      3.6.1.       Disk Diffusion Test

The antimicrobial activity of the fabricated biocomposite mats was evaluated
using the disk diffusion method. Initially, the antimicrobial properties of nisin
powder were assessed by the same test. As shown in Table 4, pure nisin exhibited
no inhibition against Gram-negative E. coli but was effective against Gram-
positive L. monocytogenes. Similarly, the CS/PVA sample (negative control)
showed no antimicrobial activity. Therefore, the inhibition zone observed in the
CS/PVA/N mat can be attributed to the incorporation of nisin.

   3.7.      Potential Application in Commercial Food Packaging

The developed double-layer mat is designed as an active component that can be
integrated into existing commercial packs rather than replacing the entire rigid or
barrier structure. It can be used as a tray liner or pad inside conventional lidded
trays, applied as a thin electrospun coating laminated onto food-contact films (e.g.,

                                                           S
PET/PE, PP, or paperboard), or employed as an inner wrap for ready-to-eat

                                                         S
products. The double-layer mat exhibited strong antimicrobial activity in both agar
                                                        E
                                                      R
diffusion and dynamic tests, confirming its effectiveness against foodborne

                                                     P
pathogens. Its layered design provided controlled release on the food-contact side


                                            IN
and moisture resistance on the outer surface. Mechanical evaluation also indicated
sufficient flexibility and strength for handling and application. Moreover, the use

                             L E
of food-grade polymers and natural bioactives, verified by structural and thermal

                           C
analyses, demonstrated that the material is both safe and stable under conditions
                          I
                        T
relevant to food packaging. In practice, the mats can be electrospun directly onto


                     A R
carrier films or supplied as precut pads, enabling direct substitution of the
absorbent pad or liner commonly used in meat, poultry, or ready-to-eat cheese and
delicatessen products with antimicrobial versions that provide in-pack protection,
particularly against L. monocytogenes in short shelf-life refrigerated foods.
Although the present findings demonstrate promising antimicrobial potential, full
commercial implementation will require additional validation, including migration
testing, sensory evaluation, and barrier performance benchmarking, which are
standard steps in qualifying new active packaging materials [5, 50, 51]. From an
industrial perspective, the double-layer mat aligns with scalable electrospinning
routes (multi-nozzle and free-surface systems demonstrated at pilot scale) and can
be integrated as drop-in liners or coated inserts on existing PET/PE or paperboard
lines, which is typically more cost-effective than full structure replacement.
Commercialization will require migration and toxicological assessments of actives,
compliance with EU and FDA food-contact frameworks, and barrier benchmarking
alongside sensory and consumer-acceptance studies for essential-oil–based
systems. These industrial aspects will be addressed in future work, including

  4. Conclusion

  This study established an electrospun double-layer antimicrobial mat in which a
  hydrophilic CS/PVA inner layer loaded with nisin and Shirazi thyme essential oil
  is combined with a hydrophobic CA/EO outer layer. A coherent set of

ACCEPTED
                          ARTICLEMANUSCRIPT
                                  IN PRESS
morphological, spectroscopic, thermal, wettability, and mechanical analyses
confirmed successful incorporation of the bioactives, process-relevant stability,
and asymmetric surface functionality. The CS/PVA-based inner layer formed bead-
free nanofibers with an average diameter of ~145 nm, while the CA/EO outer
layer exhibited thicker fibers (~270 nm), contact angles of ~95°, and contributed
to overall film integrity with an elongation at break of 21.66 ± 0.62%, indicating
adequate flexibility for handling and conversion. Across complementary
antimicrobial assays, the double-layer mat consistently inhibited both Listeria
monocytogenes and Escherichia coli. In agar diffusion tests, inhibition zones
reached 27.26 ± 1.60 mm for L. monocytogenes and 25.13 ± 1.40 mm for E. coli,
clearly outperforming single-layer controls. In the dynamic shake-flask assay, a 5
× 5 cm pad reduced L. monocytogenes by approximately 2 logs and maintained
bacterial counts below the detection limit for 48 h. The study confirms the synergy
between nisin and thyme essential oil and highlights the double-layer design’s
role in directional release.
The developed mat can be easily integrated into existing chilled food packaging
systems to control L. monocytogenes contamination. Such double-layer
electrospun systems are consistent with contemporary trends in active and
sustainable food packaging, where antimicrobial nanofiber mats are being

                                                S S
explored not only to improve microbiological safety but also to reduce food

                                               E
spoilage, product recalls, and associated food waste along the supply chain. In

                                             R
                                            P
this context, electrospun active packaging is increasingly discussed as a tool to
support circular and greener food systems and to align with broader sustainability

                                      IN
and food-security goals. Recent work on advanced electrospun structures for


                          L E
active and smart packaging, as well as analyses of their contribution to more
resilient and sustainable value chains, reinforces the industrial relevance of the

                       IC
approach demonstrated in this study.

                    RT
This work nevertheless has several limitations. Antimicrobial performance was

                  A
evaluated in broth-based model systems using two reference strains, without
testing in real food matrices or under variable storage conditions. In addition,
migration behavior and release kinetics of nisin and essential oil, sensory impacts,
barrier properties, and techno-economic aspects were not assessed. Future
studies should therefore (i) validate the mats in representative foods such as
ready-to-eat meats, cheeses, and minimally processed produce; (ii) quantify
release and migration in relation to regulatory limits and evaluate sensory
acceptability; (iii) integrate the double-layer concept with fully biodegradable
supports and scalable needleless or multi-nozzle electrospinning; and (iv) explore
incorporation of additional functionalities, such as antioxidant or colorimetric
indicator components, coupled with life-cycle and techno-economic assessments,
to move towards smart, sustainable active packaging solutions suitable for
industrial implementation.
